lessons.title: Exercise 9.2 (p.196) - Polygons
lessons.notes_html:
A polygon is a closed figure made of straight sides. It is regular when all sides and all angles are equal, otherwise irregular. It is convex when all interior angles are less than 180 degrees, and concave when one angle is greater than 180 degrees. Formulas: Sum of interior angles = (n - 2) x 180 degrees; Each interior angle of a regular polygon = (n - 2) x 180 / n degrees, where n is the number of sides.

In this exercise: 1. Identify regular and irregular polygons in the following.; 2. Identify convex and concave polygons.; 4. Calculate the sum of interior angles and each interior angle of a regular polygon.; 6. Calculate the sum of interior angles and each interior angle of the following regular polygons.

Worked Example: (i) Triangle (regular, 3 sides)

Formula used: Sum of interior angles = (n - 2) x 180 degrees.

Step 1: Sum of interior angles = (n - 2) x 180 = (3 - 2) x 180 = 180 degrees.

Step 2: Each interior angle = 180/3 = 60 degrees.

Answer: Sum = 180 degrees, each angle = 60 degrees.

Worked Example: (ii) Rectangle (4 sides)

Formula used: Sum of interior angles = (n - 2) x 180 degrees.

Step 1: Sum of interior angles = (4 - 2) x 180 = 360 degrees.

Step 2: Each interior angle = 360/4 = 90 degrees.

Answer: Sum = 360 degrees, each angle = 90 degrees. Flag: a rectangle is not a regular polygon unless it is a square (its sides need not be equal); its angles are still all 90 degrees, so the same numbers apply.

Worked Example: (iii) Heptagon (regular, 7 sides)

Formula used: Sum of interior angles = (n - 2) x 180 degrees.

Step 1: Sum of interior angles = (7 - 2) x 180 = 5 x 180 = 900 degrees.

Step 2: Each interior angle = 900/7 = 128.57 degrees (approximately).

Answer: Sum = 900 degrees, each angle = 128.57 degrees (approximately).

Worked Example: (i) 9 sides (regular nonagon)

Formula used: Sum of interior angles = (n - 2) x 180 degrees.

Step 1: Sum = (9 - 2) x 180 = 7 x 180 = 1260 degrees.

Step 2: Each interior angle = 1260/9 = 140 degrees.

Answer: Sum = 1260 degrees, each angle = 140 degrees.

Worked Example: (ii) 12 sides (regular dodecagon)

Formula used: Sum of interior angles = (n - 2) x 180 degrees.

Step 1: Sum = (12 - 2) x 180 = 10 x 180 = 1800 degrees.

Step 2: Each interior angle = 1800/12 = 150 degrees.

Answer: Sum = 1800 degrees, each angle = 150 degrees.

Worked Example: (iii) 20 sides (regular icosagon)

Formula used: Sum of interior angles = (n - 2) x 180 degrees.

Step 1: Sum = (20 - 2) x 180 = 18 x 180 = 3240 degrees.

Step 2: Each interior angle = 3240/20 = 162 degrees.

Answer: Sum = 3240 degrees, each angle = 162 degrees.

(iv) Elongated hexagon

5. Define convex and concave polygon.

A convex polygon is a polygon in which all interior angles are less than 180 degrees, so that the whole polygon bulges outward and every diagonal lies inside it. A concave polygon is a polygon in which at least one interior angle is greater than 180 degrees (a reflex angle), so that part of the polygon is pushed inward (a dent) and at least one diagonal lies outside it.

lessons.title: Exercise 9.3 (p.200) - Terms of the Circle
lessons.notes_html:
Terms of the circle: the centre is the fixed middle point; a radius joins the centre to the circle; a diameter passes through the centre and is twice the radius; a chord joins two points on the circle; the circumference is the distance around the circle; an arc is a part of the circumference.

In this exercise: 2. Describe the following terms of the circle with the help of figures.

1. Match the names of terms of the circle with the given figure.

In the given figure: the centre is the point C. The diameter is the line segment AB passing through the centre C and joining two points of the circle. A radius is the line segment from the centre C to any point on the circle, for example CA or CB. The circumference is the whole outer boundary (perimeter) of the circle. A chord is a line segment joining two points of the circle; in the figure the vertical segment to the right of the centre is a chord. The minor segment is the smaller region cut off by that chord (the shaded region in the figure). The major segment is the larger remaining region. A semi-circle is half of the circle, cut by the diameter AB.

ii. Centre of the circle

The centre is the fixed point inside the circle from which every point of the circle is at the same distance.

iv. Diameter

The diameter is a chord passing through the centre; it joins two points of the circle through the centre and is twice the radius.

ii. Segment

A segment is the region of a circle cut off by a chord: the region between the chord and its arc.

iv. Major segment

The major segment is the larger of the two regions cut off by a chord.

lessons.title: Exercise 10.1 (p.205) - Perimeter and Area of Composite Figures
lessons.notes_html:
The perimeter of a figure is the total length of its boundary. The area is the surface it covers. Formulas: Area of rectangle = length x width; Area of square = side x side; Area of triangle = 1/2 x base x height; Area of parallelogram = base x height. For a composite figure, divide it into rectangles, squares and triangles, find each area, and add them.

Worked Example: (i) Shaded square of side 12 m inside a 20 m square frame: find the perimeter and area of the shaded portion.

Formula used: Area of rectangle = l x w; Area of triangle = 1/2 x b x h.

Step 1: Perimeter = 4 x side = 4 x 12 = 48 m.

Step 2: Area = side x side = 12 x 12 = 144 m^2.

Answer: Perimeter = 48 m, area = 144 m^2.

Worked Example: (ii) L-shaped figure (top bar 10 cm wide and 5 cm tall; stem 5 cm wide; total height 15 cm): find the perimeter and area of the shaded portion.

Formula used: Area of rectangle = l x w; Area of triangle = 1/2 x b x h.

Step 1: The stem height is 15 - 5 = 10 cm.

Step 2: Perimeter (going around the outline): 10 + 15 + 5 + 10 + 5 + 5 = 50 cm.

Step 3: Area = area of top bar + area of stem = (10 x 5) + (5 x 10) = 50 + 50 = 100 cm^2.

Answer: Perimeter = 50 cm, area = 100 cm^2.

Worked Example: (iii) Two shaded diamonds of side 4 cm inside a 20 cm by 12 cm rectangle: find the perimeter and area of the shaded portion.

Formula used: Area of rectangle = l x w; Area of triangle = 1/2 x b x h.

Step 1: Perimeter of one diamond = 4 x 4 = 16 cm; two diamonds = 32 cm.

Step 2: Area of one diamond (taken as a square of side 4 cm, as labelled) = 4 x 4 = 16 cm^2; two diamonds = 32 cm^2.

Answer: Perimeter = 32 cm, area = 32 cm^2. Flag: the figure is not drawn to scale (two 4 cm diamonds cannot span the 20 cm frame); the area is computed from the labelled side length.

lessons.title: Exercise 10.3 (p.217) - Cylinders
lessons.notes_html:
A cylinder has two circular ends and a curved surface. Formulas: Curved surface area = 2 x pi x r x h; Total surface area = 2 x pi x r x (h + r); Volume = pi x r x r x h. Take pi = 22/7.

Worked Example: (i) Cylinder of length 36 cm and diameter 2.8 cm: find the total surface area and volume.

Formula used: Volume of cylinder = pi r^2 h; Total surface area = 2 pi r (h + r).

Step 1: Radius r = 2.8/2 = 1.4 cm, height h = 36 cm.

Step 2: Total surface area = 2 x (22/7) x r x (r + h) = 2 x (22/7) x 1.4 x 37.4 = 8.8 x 37.4 = 329.12 cm^2.

Step 3: Volume = (22/7) x r^2 x h = (22/7) x 1.96 x 36 = 221.76 cm^3.

Answer: Total surface area = 329.12 cm^2, volume = 221.76 cm^3.

Worked Example: (ii) Cylinder of height 18 cm and diameter 9 cm: find the total surface area and volume.

Formula used: Volume of cylinder = pi r^2 h; Total surface area = 2 pi r (h + r).

Step 1: Radius r = 9/2 = 4.5 cm (the 9 cm arrow spans the full width of the cylinder, so it is the diameter), height h = 18 cm.

Step 2: Total surface area = 2 x (22/7) x 4.5 x (4.5 + 18) = (198/7) x 22.5 = 636.43 cm^2.

Step 3: Volume = (22/7) x 4.5 x 4.5 x 18 = 8019/7 = 1145.57 cm^3.

Answer: Total surface area = 636.43 cm^2, volume = 1145.57 cm^3.

Worked Example: (iii) Cylinder of radius 0.7 cm and height 5.6 cm: find the total surface area and volume.

Formula used: Volume of cylinder = pi r^2 h; Total surface area = 2 pi r (h + r).

Step 1: Total surface area = 2 x (22/7) x 0.7 x (0.7 + 5.6) = 4.4 x 6.3 = 27.72 cm^2.

Step 2: Volume = (22/7) x 0.7 x 0.7 x 5.6 = 1.54 x 5.6 = 8.624 cm^3.

Answer: Total surface area = 27.72 cm^2, volume = 8.624 cm^3.

A right triangular prism has two triangular faces and three rectangular faces. Formulas: Volume = 1/2 x b x h x l; Total surface area = b x h + l x (b + h + s), where b and h are the base and height of the triangular face, s is its slant side and l is the length of the prism.

Worked Example: (i) Right triangular prism with b = 8 cm, h = 6 cm, s = 10 cm, l = 4 cm: find the surface area and volume.

Formula used: Volume of triangular prism = 1/2 x b x h x l.

Step 1: Check: 8^2 + 6^2 = 64 + 36 = 100 = 10^2, so the triangular face is right-angled.

Step 2: Surface area = (8 x 6) + 4 x (8 + 6 + 10) = 48 + 96 = 144 cm^2.

Step 3: Volume = (1/2) x 8 x 6 x 4 = 96 cm^3.

Answer: Surface area = 144 cm^2, volume = 96 cm^3.

Worked Example: (ii) Right triangular prism with b = 12 cm, h = 5 cm, s = 13 cm, l = 6 cm: find the surface area and volume.

Formula used: Volume of triangular prism = 1/2 x b x h x l.

Step 1: Check: 12^2 + 5^2 = 144 + 25 = 169 = 13^2, so the triangular face is right-angled.

Step 2: Surface area = (12 x 5) + 6 x (12 + 5 + 13) = 60 + 180 = 240 cm^2.

Step 3: Volume = (1/2) x 12 x 5 x 6 = 180 cm^3.

Answer: Surface area = 240 cm^2, volume = 180 cm^3.

Worked Example: 2. A right triangular mosquito net (camping tent) made of nylon is 8 m long. The lengths of the triangular face are 3 m, 4 m and 5 m. Find the total surface area and volume of the tent.

Formula used: Volume of triangular prism = 1/2 x b x h x l.

Step 1: Check: 3^2 + 4^2 = 9 + 16 = 25 = 5^2, so the triangular face is right-angled with base 3 m and height 4 m.

Step 2: Area of one triangular face = (1/2) x 3 x 4 = 6 m^2.

Step 3: Total surface area = 2 x 6 + 8 x (3 + 4 + 5) = 12 + 96 = 108 m^2.

Step 4: Volume = 6 x 8 = 48 m^3.

Answer: Total surface area = 108 m^2, volume = 48 m^3. Flag: the figure labels one side '4cm'; the question text gives 4 m, which is used.

Note: Formulas used: total surface area = b x h + l x (b + h + s), where b and h are the base and height of the triangular face, s is its slant side and l is the prism length; volume = (1/2) x b x h x l.

lessons.title: Exercise 11.1 (p.233) - Angles in Triangles
lessons.notes_html:
Formulas: the sum of the angles in a triangle = 180 degrees; an exterior angle of a triangle = sum of the two opposite interior angles. To find an unknown angle, add the known angles and subtract from 180 degrees.

In this exercise: 1. Calculate the unknown angles in the following.; 2. Calculate the unknown angles in a triangle.; 3. Calculate the unknown angles in a triangle.

Worked Example: (i) Right triangle ABC, right angle at B, interior angle at C = 45 degrees, exterior angle at C = x, angle at A = a.

Formula used: Angles in a triangle add to 180 degrees.

Step 1: Exterior angle at C: x = 180 - 45 = 135 degrees.

Step 2: Angle a = 180 - 90 - 45 = 45 degrees.

Answer: a = 45 degrees, x = 135 degrees.

Worked Example: (iii) Triangle ABC with angle at A = 50 degrees, angle at B = 80 degrees, interior angle at C = c, exterior angle at C = x.

Formula used: Angles in a triangle add to 180 degrees.

Step 1: Interior angle c = 180 - 50 - 80 = 50 degrees.

Step 2: Exterior angle x = 180 - 50 = 130 degrees.

Answer: c = 50 degrees, x = 130 degrees.

Worked Example: (i) Isosceles triangle ABC with AB = AC (marked equal) and angle at B = 60 degrees.

Formula used: Angles in a triangle add to 180 degrees.

Step 1: Base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal, so angle at C = angle at B = 60 degrees.

Step 2: Angle at A = 180 - 60 - 60 = 60 degrees.

Answer: Angles: A = 60 degrees, B = 60 degrees, C = 60 degrees (the triangle is equilateral in effect).

Worked Example: (iii) Triangle with angle at the top vertex = 30 degrees and angle at the bottom-right vertex = 20 degrees; find the angle at the bottom-left vertex.

Formula used: Angles in a triangle add to 180 degrees.

Step 1: The unknown angle = 180 - 30 - 20 = 130 degrees.

Answer: The bottom-left angle = 130 degrees (obtuse).

Worked Example: (i) Triangle ABC with AB = BC = CA = 3 cm and all angles marked x.

Formula used: Angles in a triangle add to 180 degrees.

Step 1: All three sides are equal, so the triangle is equilateral and all angles are equal: x = 180/3 = 60 degrees.

Answer: Each angle x = 60 degrees.

Worked Example: (iii) Right triangle ABC, right angle at C, angle at B = 2x, angle at A = x.

Formula used: Angles in a triangle add to 180 degrees.

Step 1: x + 2x + 90 = 180, so 3x = 90 and x = 30 degrees.

Step 2: Angle at B = 2x = 60 degrees.

Answer: x = 30 degrees, angle at B = 60 degrees.

lessons.title: Exercise 11.2 (p.237) - Construction of Triangles
lessons.notes_html:
To construct a triangle, draw the given side with a ruler, then construct the given angles with a compass (or mark the given side lengths with arcs from the endpoints), and join the intersection point to the endpoints. Follow the given data exactly: side-side-side, side-angle-side or angle-side-angle, as the question states.

1. Construct an equilateral triangle PQR when PQ = QR = RP = 4 cm.

Draw PQ = 4 cm. With the compass open to 4 cm, draw an arc from P and an arc from Q; they intersect at R. Join PR and QR. Triangle PQR is equilateral with all sides 4 cm.

3. Construct an isosceles triangle XYZ when XZ = YZ = 4 cm and XY = 3 cm.

Draw XY = 3 cm. With the compass open to 4 cm, draw an arc from X and an arc from Y; they intersect at Z. Join XZ and YZ. Triangle XYZ is isosceles with XZ = YZ = 4 cm.

4. Construct an isosceles triangle ABC when AB = 4 cm, angle A = 30 degrees and angle B = 30 degrees.

Draw AB = 4 cm. Construct an angle of 30 degrees at A and an angle of 30 degrees at B with the compass. The two arms intersect at C. Triangle ABC is isosceles with AC = BC and angle at C = 180 - 30 - 30 = 120 degrees.

5. Construct a scalene triangle PQR when PQ = 5 cm, angle P = 120 degrees and PR = 6 cm.

Draw PQ = 5 cm. Construct an angle of 120 degrees at P with the compass. Mark R on the arm so that PR = 6 cm. Join QR. Triangle PQR is scalene (all sides different).

7. Construct an acute-angled triangle PQR when PQ = 4 cm, angle P = 45 degrees and angle Q = 60 degrees.

Draw PQ = 4 cm. Construct an angle of 45 degrees at P and an angle of 60 degrees at Q with the compass. The two arms intersect at R. Angle at R = 180 - 45 - 60 = 75 degrees, so all angles are acute and triangle PQR is acute-angled.

Note: General method: draw the given side with a ruler, construct the given angles with a compass (or mark the given side lengths with arcs from the endpoints), and join the intersection point to the endpoints.

lessons.title: Exercise 11.3 (p.242) - Lines of Symmetry
lessons.notes_html:
A line of symmetry divides a figure into two equal halves that match exactly when folded. A square has 4 lines of symmetry, a rectangle has 2, an equilateral triangle has 3, an isosceles triangle has 1, and a circle has infinitely many.

In this exercise: 1. Identify and draw a line of symmetry of the following figures.

Green parallelogram

No line of symmetry: a general parallelogram (not a rectangle or rhombus) cannot be folded onto itself along any line.

Division symbol (a horizontal bar with one dot above and one dot below)

Two lines of symmetry: one vertical line through the middle and one horizontal line through the middle.

Wheel (circle with spokes)

Infinitely many lines of symmetry: any line through the centre of the circle divides it into two identical halves.

Cat face (photograph)

One line of symmetry: a vertical line through the middle of the face, between the eyes and ears.

Light bulb

One line of symmetry: a vertical line through the centre of the bulb and its base.

options: It divides the figure into two unequal parts
It rotates the figure by 180 degrees
It divides the figure into two equal halves that match exactly when folded
It divides the figure into three equal parts
mcqs.why: The notes define: a line of symmetry divides a figure into two equal halves that match exactly when folded.

lessons.title: Exercise 11.4 (p.248) - Translation
lessons.notes_html:
In a translation, every point of a figure moves by the same distance in the same direction: (x, y) moves to (x + a, y + b) for a move of a units horizontally and b units vertically. The shape and size do not change. Note: this unit's review is printed with the heading 'Review Exercise 4'; it is the Unit 11 review.

Worked Example: (i) Triangle ABC with A(-7, 3), B(-5, 7), C(-3, 3) is translated to A'(4, -7), B'(6, -3), C'(8, -7). Describe the translation and write the coordinate equation.

Formula used: (x, y) -> (x + a, y + b).

Step 1: A to A': x changes from -7 to 4 (11 units right), y changes from 3 to -7 (10 units down).

Step 2: Check B: -5 + 11 = 6 and 7 - 10 = -3. Check C: -3 + 11 = 8 and 3 - 10 = -7.

lessons.title: Exercise 12.3 (p.280) - Discrete, Continuous, Grouped and Ungrouped Data
lessons.notes_html:
Discrete data takes countable whole-number values, for example the number of students. Continuous data can take any value in a range, for example height or weight. Ungrouped data is listed as single values; grouped data is arranged in class intervals.

In this exercise: 1. Identify the discrete and continuous data in the following.; 2. Identify the grouped and ungrouped data.

(iv) The number of rooms in 6 students' homes: 6, 7, 8, 2, 9, 3.

Discrete data: numbers of rooms are whole-number counts.

(i) Grade VII, top 5 students' marks in Geography test out of 50 marks: 40, 35, 45, 36, 39.

3. Write the difference between continuous and discrete data with the help of three examples.

Discrete data takes only whole-number, countable values that cannot be subdivided: for example, the number of students in a class (50), the number of wickets in a match (4), and marks out of 50 (49). Continuous data takes any value within a range, including decimals, because it comes from measurement: for example, the height of a student (5.3 feet), the weight of a teacher (74.4 kg), and the rainfall in a month (25.5 mm).

lessons.title: Exercise 12.5 (p.295) - Mean, Median and Mode
lessons.notes_html:
Formulas: Mean = Sum of values / Number of values; Median = the middle value when the data is arranged in order (for an even count, the mean of the two middle values); Mode = the value that occurs most often.

Worked Example: 1. (i) Calculate the mean, median and mode of 25, 30, 40, 35, 45, 50, 60.

Formula used: Mean = Sum / Count; Median = middle value; Mode = most frequent.

Step 1: Mean: sum = 25 + 30 + 40 + 35 + 45 + 50 + 60 = 285; mean = 285/7 = 40.71 (approximately).

Step 2: Median: arrange in ascending order: 25, 30, 35, 40, 45, 50, 60; the middle value (4th of 7) is 40.

Step 3: Mode: no value repeats, so there is no mode.

Answer: Mean = 40.71 (approximately), median = 40, no mode.

Worked Example: 1. (ii) Calculate the mean, median and mode of 70, 72, 71, 72, 73, 74, 75.

Formula used: Mean = Sum / Count; Median = middle value; Mode = most frequent.

Step 1: Mean: sum = 70 + 72 + 71 + 72 + 73 + 74 + 75 = 507; mean = 507/7 = 72.43 (approximately).

Step 2: Median: arrange in ascending order: 70, 71, 72, 72, 73, 74, 75; the middle value is 72.

Step 3: Mode: 72 occurs twice, more than any other value.

Answer: Mean = 72.43 (approximately), median = 72, mode = 72.

Worked Example: 1. (iii) Calculate the mean, median and mode of 110, 120, 130, 140, 150, 160, 150, 160.

Step 3: Mode: 150 and 160 each occur twice, so there are two modes.

Answer: Mean = 140, median = 145, modes = 150 and 160.

lessons.title: Exercise 12.6 (p.304) - Probability
lessons.notes_html:
Probability measures how likely an event is. Formula: P(event) = Number of favourable outcomes / Total number of possible outcomes. An action that produces different outcomes is an experiment; all possible outcomes form the sample space; one specific result is an outcome; a subset of the sample space is an event. A certain event always happens and an impossible event never happens.

In this exercise: 1. Explain the following terms with an example.; 2. Categorize the following events (certain event, impossible event, complement of an event).

Worked Example: 5. Waseem and Waqar spin the given spinner (three equal sectors: red, green and blue). Find the probability of green and red colors.

Formula used: P(event) = Favourable outcomes / Total outcomes.

Step 1: The spinner has 3 equal sectors, so each colour has probability 1/3.

Step 2: Probability of green = 1/3.

Step 3: Probability of red = 1/3.

Answer: P(green) = 1/3, P(red) = 1/3.

Worked Example: 6. Two friends Manahil and Alia tossed a coin. Alia chose the head and Manahil chose the tail. Find the probability.

Formula used: P(event) = Favourable outcomes / Total outcomes.

Step 1: Sample space = {Head, Tail}, two equally likely outcomes.

Step 2: Probability that Alia (head) wins = 1/2.

Step 3: Probability that Manahil (tail) wins = 1/2.

Answer: P(Alia wins) = 1/2, P(Manahil wins) = 1/2.

Worked Example: 7. Three friends Naeem, Kaleem and Kareem rolled a die and got the following events: A = even numbers, B = prime numbers, C = not even nor prime. Find the probability of events A, B, C.

Formula used: P(event) = Favourable outcomes / Total outcomes.

Step 1: Sample space = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} (6 outcomes).

Step 2: A = {2, 4, 6}, so P(A) = 3/6 = 1/2.

Step 3: B = {2, 3, 5}, so P(B) = 3/6 = 1/2.

Step 4: C = {1} (1 is the only number from 1 to 6 that is neither even nor prime), so P(C) = 1/6.

Answer: P(A) = 1/2, P(B) = 1/2, P(C) = 1/6.

(i) Certain event

An event that is sure to happen: for example, the sun rising in the east tomorrow. Its probability is 1.

(i) The Pakistan football team win the toss against Iran.

An ordinary uncertain event: it may or may not happen. Its complement is 'the Pakistan football team do not win the toss'.

(iv) Sun is the main source of energy in the universe.

Certain event: it is always true.

(vi) During rolling a die, Sidra missed the chance to roll the die.

Flag: no die outcome occurs here at all, so as an event of the die roll it is an impossible event (none of the outcomes 1-6 occurs).

4. Musfira is rolling a die. Write the sample space, events and outcomes for it.

Sample space S = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}. Events include: getting an even number {2, 4, 6}, getting an odd number {1, 3, 5}, and getting a prime number {2, 3, 5}. Outcomes: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 or 6.

mcqs.q: What is the formula for the probability of an event?
options: Total outcomes divided by favourable outcomes
Number of favourable outcomes / Total number of possible outcomes
1 minus the total number of outcomes
mcqs.why: The notes give the formula: P(event) = Number of favourable outcomes / Total number of possible outcomes.

mcqs.q: A spinner has three equal sectors: red, green and blue. What is the probability of green?
mcqs.why: P(green) = Number of favourable outcomes / Total outcomes = 1/3, because the spinner has 3 equal sectors.

mcqs.q: A spinner has three equal sectors: red, green and blue. What is the probability of red?
mcqs.why: P(red) = Number of favourable outcomes / Total outcomes = 1/3, because each colour has probability 1/3 on the 3-sector spinner.

mcqs.q: Alia chose head and Manahil chose tail when a coin was tossed. What is the probability that Alia (head) wins?
mcqs.why: Sample space = {Head, Tail}, two equally likely outcomes, so P(Alia wins) = 1/2 = favourable outcomes / total outcomes.

mcqs.q: For a die, event A = even numbers {2, 4, 6}. What is P(A)?
mcqs.why: P(A) = Number of favourable outcomes / Total outcomes = 3/6 = 1/2, because A = {2, 4, 6} has 3 outcomes out of 6.

mcqs.q: For a die, event B = prime numbers {2, 3, 5}. What is P(B)?
mcqs.why: P(B) = Number of favourable outcomes / Total outcomes = 3/6 = 1/2, because B = {2, 3, 5} has 3 outcomes out of 6.

mcqs.q: For a die, event C = not even nor prime, which is {1}. What is P(C)?
mcqs.why: P(C) = Number of favourable outcomes / Total outcomes = 1/6, because 1 is the only number from 1 to 6 that is neither even nor prime.

mcqs.q: What is the probability of a certain event, such as the sun rising in the east tomorrow?
mcqs.why: The notes state a certain event is sure to happen, for example the sun rising in the east tomorrow, and its probability is 1.

mcqs.why: The notes state the sample space for rolling a die is S = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}, all possible outcomes of the experiment.

options: The Pakistan football team do not win the toss

lessons.notes_html:
Review of Unit 1: rational numbers, number line, place value, rounding, fraction types and the commutative, associative and distributive laws.

In this exercise: 1. Choose the correct option.

Worked Example: 2. Construct a frequency table for the given data: 11, 12, 13, 11, 12, 14, 15, 13, 14, 15, 16, 14, 15, 14, 10, 10, 11, 10, 11, 12, 16, 14, 15, 16, 12, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15.

Formula used: See the formulas in Lessons 1 to 5 of this unit.

Step 1: Count each value: 10 occurs 3 times, 11 occurs 5 times, 12 occurs 5 times, 13 occurs 3 times, 14 occurs 6 times, 15 occurs 5 times, 16 occurs 3 times.

Step 2: Check: 3 + 5 + 5 + 3 + 6 + 5 + 3 = 30 values, matching the data.

Answer: Frequency table: 10: 3; 11: 5; 12: 5; 13: 3; 14: 6; 15: 5; 16: 3. Total = 30.

Worked Example: 3. Hasnain's cricket team scored the following runs in a cricket match: 50, 30, 40, 25, 15, 35, 25, 20, 30, 30. Calculate the mean, median and mode.

Formula used: See the formulas in Lessons 1 to 5 of this unit.

Step 1: Mean: sum = 50 + 30 + 40 + 25 + 15 + 35 + 25 + 20 + 30 + 30 = 300; mean = 300/10 = 30.

Step 2: Median: arrange in ascending order: 15, 20, 25, 25, 30, 30, 30, 35, 40, 50; the two middle values are both 30, so the median is 30.

Step 3: Mode: 30 occurs three times, more than any other value.

Answer: Mean = 30, median = 30, mode = 30.

Worked Example: 4. Sidra rolled a die. Find the probability of getting (i) a number less than six, (ii) a number that is a factor of six, (iii) prime numbers.

Formula used: See the formulas in Lessons 1 to 5 of this unit.

Step 1: Sample space = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} (6 outcomes).

Step 2: (i) Numbers less than six: {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}, so probability = 5/6.

Step 3: (ii) Factors of six: {1, 2, 3, 6}, so probability = 4/6 = 2/3.

Step 4: (iii) Prime numbers: {2, 3, 5}, so probability = 3/6 = 1/2.

Answer: P(less than six) = 5/6, P(factor of six) = 2/3, P(prime) = 1/2.
